scenes.title: dbt Snapshots (SCD Type 2)
scenes.narration: This lesson explains dbt snapshots, the feature that captures how records change over time using the slowly changing dimension type two pattern.

scenes.title: The problem snapshots solve
bullets: Source systems overwrite records in place
History is lost the moment a value changes
Snapshots preserve every version over time
scenes.narration: Many source systems update records in place, so when a customer changes their address the old value is simply overwritten and lost forever. Snapshots solve this by watching a table and recording a new version of a row every time it changes, preserving the full history that the source itself discards.

scenes.title: How SCD Type 2 works
steps: Close the old version with an end date
Insert the new version as current
scenes.narration: The slowly changing dimension type two pattern works by never deleting. When dbt detects that a tracked row has changed, it closes out the previous version by stamping it with a valid-to date, then inserts the new values as a fresh current record. The result is a full timeline where you can ask what any record looked like on any past date.

scenes.title: Defining a snapshot
scenes.narration: This snapshot tracks the customers source table. The unique_key tells dbt how to identify a single logical record across versions. The timestamp strategy means dbt decides a row has changed by comparing the updated_at column, which is efficient when the source reliably maintains such a column. Running dbt snapshot on a schedule is what builds up the history over time.

scenes.title: timestamp versus check strategy
scenes.narration: dbt offers two change-detection strategies. The timestamp strategy relies on an updated_at column and is cheap and precise, but only when the source maintains that column faithfully. The check strategy instead compares the actual values of a chosen list of columns, which works even when no reliable timestamp exists, at the cost of a bit more compute on every run.

scenes.title: The metadata dbt adds
bullets: dbt_valid_from marks when a version began
dbt_valid_to is null for the current version
scenes.narration: Every snapshot table gains helpful metadata columns. dbt_valid_from records when a version became active, dbt_valid_to records when it was superseded and is null for the current row, and dbt_scd_id gives each historical version its own stable identifier. Filtering where dbt_valid_to is null gives you the latest state of every record.

scenes.text: Snapshots turn overwrite-in-place sources into full SCD Type 2 history, letting you reconstruct exactly what a record looked like at any point in time.
scenes.narration: The essential point is that snapshots transform overwrite-in-place source tables into complete slowly changing dimension type two history, giving you the power to reconstruct exactly what any record looked like at any moment in the past.
